I checked the built output for the draft's slug: it appears nowhere in dist, including the feed and the sitemap. The draft page itself is still reachable in the dev server for previews.

I added a test for the helper with one draft and two published posts.

summary: Looked at the build warnings that piled up after the updates and removed the ones that mattered, leaving a clean build log.
body:
The build log had grown to 24 warnings. I grouped them. Nine were deprecated option notices from the image package, seven were missing alt attributes in older posts, five were the tag case warnings and three were duplicate slug aliases in the redirects.

For the image option, I replaced the deprecated format setting with the new name. The alt warnings pointed at seven images in the early posts; I wrote descriptions after viewing each image and the user approved them.

The duplicate aliases were real: two old URLs redirected to the same post twice, which Netlify tolerates but the file was confusing. I removed the duplicates and tested the redirects with curl on ten old URLs from the migration list, all returning 301 to the right place.

The tag warnings were fixed by normalizing the remaining front matter. The build log is now empty apart from the timing lines.

summary: Investigated a slow image build after adding a big photo to a draft, and set a maximum source size with a script that warns before the build gets slow.
body:
The build jumped from 33 to 71 seconds after the user added photos for the homelab rack draft. Two JPEG files were 6000 pixels wide and about 9 MB each.

The image pipeline generated five widths and two formats for each, so these two files cost more than all other images together. I resized the sources at the origin to 2400 pixels wide, which is more than the largest display width of 1600 with room for high density screens. The files fell to about 700 KB each and the build returned to 34 seconds.

To avoid repeating this, I wrote a small script, check-images.mjs, that scans the content folder and fails on any source over 3000 pixels wide or 2 MB. It is part of the CI step before the build. The error message prints the file, its size and the resize command.

I ran it against all images in the repository. Only those two had been over the limit. One older PNG screenshot was 1.8 MB, near the limit, and I recompressed it to 600 KB without visible change.

The user checked the photos on the draft page and found them sharp. I also checked that the lazy loading attributes were still present and that the first image of the post is not lazy loaded.

Nothing else is pending on this, and the draft itself is still the user's work.

summary: Added a Netlify deploy preview check that runs the link checker on a built site, and fixed three broken internal links it found in older posts.
body:
The user wanted to know whether old posts still link to pages that exist. I added a link checker script that reads the built HTML in dist and verifies every internal href and image src against the files and the redirect list.

The first run found three broken links: two pointing to a tag page that no longer exists after the tag normalization, and one to an anchor in the queue post whose heading had been renamed. I fixed the three links in the posts.

External links are not checked, because that makes the build flaky. The script runs in CI after the build and takes about two seconds.

summary: Wrote the README section on dark mode, the image limits and the link check, so the next person knows the site's checks without reading the scripts.
body:
The README had grown stale. I added a section on the theme variables and where the dark values live, how the head script and the toggle work, and how the Shiki dual theme is configured.

A second section lists the CI checks in order: sample type-check, image size check, build, link check. Each has the command to run it locally and what a failure looks like.

I also listed the decision to stay on the current Tailwind major version, with a pointer to the notes of the scratch migration. The user read it and asked for no changes.

summary: Fixed the comment function failing for one reader because a trailing space in the email field was rejected by validation, and added trimming.
body:
A reader wrote to the user that the form kept saying the email address was invalid. The log of rejected requests, with the score logging added earlier, showed a value ending in a space, probably pasted from a phone keyboard.

The validation used a strict pattern on the raw field. I trimmed all text fields on the server before validation and in the form script before submit. The error message for a bad email stays the same.

I added three tests: trailing space, leading space and a tab. All fourteen function tests passed locally, and again after the deploy through a real request from curl. The spam score of the trimmed request was unchanged.

summary: Looked into a slow first paint on the archive page and found that it loaded every post's cover image at full size; it now uses the optimized small version with lazy loading.
body:
A reader said the archive page felt slow on a phone. I measured it with a throttled connection and saw that the page transferred about 4 MB. Nearly all of it was cover images.

The archive template used the original cover file instead of the optimized one that the post layout uses. So every thumbnail was downloaded at full size and scaled down by the browser. I switched the template to the image component with a fixed width of 320 pixels and WebP output.

I also set lazy loading on all thumbnails except the first three, which are visible on load. After the change the page transferred about 380 KB. The layout did not shift, because the component sets width and height.

I checked the dark mode version and the feed. Both were unchanged, since the feed does not use the archive template. One older post had no cover image and showed a broken box. I added a plain placeholder for that case. The build time did not change noticeably. I added a note about the thumbnail size to the README section on image limits.

summary: Reviewed the finished monitoring draft end to end, finding a wrong alert threshold, an outdated flag and a broken heading anchor, and the user decided to hold it back.
body:
I went through the full draft against the user's actual config files. Most of it matched, but three things did not.

The alert rule in the text said a disk alert fires at 90 percent, while the rule file used 85 percent with a ten minute wait. I corrected the text to match the file, as the file is what he runs. A second command still used an old flag that I had flagged in the first review, and he had not fixed it yet. I changed it.

The heading Alerting and routing had a duplicate id with another heading, which broke the table of contents link. I renamed the second heading.

The code samples check passed. The image check passed after last time's resizing. The link checker found one dead anchor, which was the heading problem.

There was a larger question. The post says the setup needs about 400 MB of memory, but the user had measured that only on a quiet day. I ran the stack for an hour here and saw about 520 MB at peak while the dashboards were open. I gave him both numbers.

He thought about it and decided to hold the post back until he has run it for a few weeks on the real machine and can quote a better figure. The draft stays unpublished with a draft flag, and the helper keeps it out of lists, the feed and the sitemap.

I saved the review notes in the drafts folder beside the file so the work can restart later.

summary: Held a review of the sitemap after the user asked whether old redirected URLs are listed, and found three redirected paths in it that are now removed.
body:
The user asked whether the sitemap still lists the old URLs that redirect to the new ones. I opened the generated sitemap and compared it with the redirects file. Three old paths were in the sitemap, all from the time of the move to Astro.

They came from a hand-written list of extra pages in the config that nobody had updated. I removed the three entries. The sitemap now contains only the canonical address of each published post and page.

I also checked that drafts do not appear, which the earlier filter fix covers. The held-back monitoring draft is correctly absent. Next I ran the link checker against the built site, and it found no broken links and no links to redirected paths.

I looked at the canonical tags as well. Every post points to its own address without a trailing slash difference, which matches the redirect rules. One page, the thank-you page of the comment form, had no noindex tag. I added it so that it stays out of search results and out of the sitemap. The build passed and the sitemap has three entries fewer than before.

summary: Fixed the RSS feed showing posts in the wrong order after the user edited an old post's date field, by sorting on the published date and adding an updated field.
body:
The user fixed a typo in an older post and changed its date field to say when he edited it. The post then jumped to the top of the feed and readers saw it as new.

The feed sorted by the single date field. I introduced an optional updated field in the front matter schema. The date field now always means first publication, and updated is shown on the post page as a small line under the title when present.

The feed items use the date for ordering and the pubDate, so edits no longer reorder them. I restored the old post's original date from the git history of the file and put the edit time in updated.

I rebuilt and compared the feed with the one from before the edit. The item order matches again. I validated the feed with a feed validator and had no errors.

The schema change is checked by Astro at build, so a wrong value fails loudly. I also added the updated date to the post structured data so search engines see the edit.

Two other posts had a date later than their real publication, from the same kind of edit. I did not change them without asking, and I listed them for the user.

summary: Corrected the two other posts with edited dates, then audited the whole site's front matter against the schema and fixed twelve small inconsistencies.
body:
The user confirmed the original dates of the two posts listed in the last session, and I restored them from git history, moving the edit time into the new updated field. The feed order is now stable.

Then I wrote a script that reads all front matter and reports problems the Astro schema allows. It found twelve. Four posts had descriptions longer than 160 characters, which the social card cuts off. Three had tags in a different order or with trailing spaces. Two had an image field pointing to a file that exists only in a different size. Three had no alt text for the cover.

I fixed the descriptions by shortening them and showed the user the new texts for the four posts, since the descriptions are his words. He changed one of my proposals. The tag and image issues were mechanical and I fixed them directly.

I ran the full CI sequence locally: sample check, image check, front matter audit, build and link check. It all passed. The build took 34 seconds.

I made the audit script part of CI, with a limit of 160 characters for descriptions and a required alt for the cover. The failure message names the file and the field.

I also noted in the README that the date field means first publication and that updated is for later edits, so this confusion does not return.

summary: Did a last cleanup pass on the repository: removed unused dependencies and scripts, pinned Node, and wrote a summary of the site's state and open items.
body:
The user asked for a tidy-up because he will not be working on the site much for a while. I ran a dependency check and found four packages that nothing imported any more, left from the generator migration and the first spam tests. I removed them and the lockfile shrank by about 300 entries.

I found three npm scripts that referred to files that no longer exist, and removed them. One old Netlify redirect rule pointed at a path that was served by the earlier generator, and the link checker confirmed that nothing uses it. I kept it because old external links may still exist, and added a comment saying so.

I pinned the Node version in .nvmrc and in the Netlify settings to the one the build runs on, so a platform default change cannot break the build. I tested a clean install and build from a fresh clone: 52 seconds including the install, and all checks passed.

The state summary in the README now lists what is done: the Astro move, redirects, feed, series navigation, comment form with spam rules, dark mode, and the CI checks. It lists the open items too: the monitoring draft that is held back until the user has better memory figures, the postponed Tailwind major update with its notes, and the archive pagination threshold.

The user read the summary and accepted it. The deploy from main succeeded and the live site matches the last preview.

summary: Started a post on queue backpressure with the user by outlining the argument and checking the code samples from his old worker notes against a small test run.
body:
The user wants a post about backpressure in job queues, aimed at readers who have only used a queue as a buffer. We went through his notes and cut them into an outline: the problem of an unbounded queue, bounded queues with blocking producers, load shedding, and a closing section on measuring queue age rather than depth.

I ran the three code samples from his notes. Two worked as written. The third, a producer that waits on a semaphore, had a release in the wrong branch and leaked a permit on error, so the demo hung after about forty failures. I fixed it in the draft and told the user what changed.

The draft is at src/content/posts/queue-backpressure.md with draft: true in the front matter. I checked that the new draft filter keeps it out of the archive, feed and sitemap, and it does. Open items: the user will write the intro, and I will build a small chart of queue depth under load for the middle section.

Nothing was published and no site code changed.

summary: Checked the queue backpressure draft's code samples against a small test run and found two of the user's old worker snippets no longer behave the way the outline claims.
body:
The user wants a post on queue backpressure, so tonight's session started from his outline and the old worker notes he keeps in a text file. I pulled the three code samples out of the notes into a scratch folder outside the content directory, so nothing could leak into the build or the feed. Each sample got a tiny harness: a producer that pushes jobs at a fixed rate, a worker with a fixed service time, and a counter that prints queue depth once per second.

The first sample, an unbounded in-memory queue, behaved as the outline says. With the producer at 200 jobs per second and the worker at 120, depth grew by about 80 per second and memory climbed steadily during a 60 second run. That sample works as the opening example of the problem.

The second sample, a bounded queue that blocks the producer when full, also worked, but the notes said it drops nothing. In the run it did drop nothing, yet the producer's effective rate fell to the worker's 120 per second, which is the point of backpressure. I suggested the post show that measured rate next to the configured rate so the reader sees the effect rather than taking it on trust.

The third sample, the one that rejects new jobs when the queue is full, had a real bug. It checked the length and then pushed in two separate steps, and under two producers the depth overshot the limit of 100 and reached 107 in one run. I rewrote it to check and push in one synchronous step and the overshoot disappeared across five runs. I did not change the user's prose, only left a note beside the paragraph that describes this sample.

The fourth item in the outline, a drain-on-shutdown example, was only a sketch with no code. I wrote a minimal version that stops accepting jobs, waits for the queue to empty and exits, and it finished cleanly with 100 queued jobs in about 0.8 seconds. Whether to include it is the user's decision, since the post may already be long enough.

I saved the raw output of every run as text files next to the samples, with the exact command lines at the top of each. The numbers in the draft should be taken from those files only, because the notes contained a few figures that nobody could trace back to a run. Two such figures, a claimed 30 percent latency drop and a queue depth of 500, appear in the outline and match nothing I measured.

Open items are to ask the user whether he remembers where those two figures came from, to decide on the shutdown example, and to move the samples into the post's example folder once the code is settled. Next session will be a review of his first full draft against the saved outputs.

summary: Reviewed the user's first full backpressure draft and corrected two numbers in the text that did not match the saved simulation output.
body:
The user finished the draft in the evening and asked for a review. I read it against the simulation output and the charts.

Two figures were wrong. The text said the unbounded queue reached 20,000 items, but the saved run shows about 15,000. The text also said the bounded queue held waits under 2 seconds, while the run shows 3. I corrected both and left a note in the draft so he sees the change.

Other findings were small: one code block lacked a language tag so it rendered without highlighting, a heading was used twice which broke an anchor, and the paragraph about load shedding promised a table that does not exist. I raised the table question with him instead of inventing one. He decided to drop the promise from the sentence.

The post reads well and is about 1,400 words. It stays a draft until he rereads the corrected numbers tomorrow.

summary: Published the backpressure post after the user's last edits, then fixed the missing alt text on both charts and checked the feed entry.
body:
The user reread the draft and made a few wording changes, mostly in the conclusion. I flipped draft to false and set the published date, then ran the build and the link checker. Both were clean.

After the deploy I checked the live page. The charts load with lazy loading and the right sizes, but both had empty alt attributes because I had forgotten them when converting from SVG. That is the same slip as the homelab post. I wrote real descriptions that state what each chart shows, including the end values, and redeployed.

The feed entry contained absolute image URLs this time, so the earlier feed fix holds. The sitemap lists the post once.

To avoid this a third time I added a check to the existing image script: it now warns when a Markdown image has empty alt text. It found no other cases in older posts. The check runs with the other pre-build checks and takes under a second.

summary: Started the Postgres index post by collecting the user's notes on partial and covering indexes and rebuilding the example table with a seed script.
body:
The next planned post is about Postgres indexes: when a partial index beats a full one, and what a covering index changes in the plan. The user's notes are long and uneven, so I first sorted them into three themes and flagged two claims that need proof.

For examples I extended the orders seed script that the EXPLAIN post used. It now creates one million rows with a status column where about 2 percent are pending. I checked the table size and the plan before any index: a sequential scan of about 120 ms for pending orders.

Then I built the indexes. A full index on status brought the query to roughly 9 ms. A partial index on pending orders brought it to 4 ms and was about 40 times smaller on disk, 2 MB compared with 30 MB. I saved each plan to a text file in the post folder.

The covering index claim from his notes needs a vacuum first, because index-only scans depend on the visibility map. Without it the plan showed heap fetches for every row. I added a vacuum step to the script and the index-only scan appeared.

I wrote the outline into the draft and left the prose to the user. Everything stays unpublished.

summary: Corrected the index post draft after the user's first pass, replacing two plan excerpts and rewording a claim about index-only scans that only holds after a vacuum.
body:
The user wrote most of the post in the afternoon and I reviewed it in the evening against the saved plans.

Two excerpts were pasted from an earlier run on a smaller table, so row counts and timings did not match the text. I replaced them with the saved output. The claim that a covering index always avoids reading the table was too strong. It holds only when the visibility map is current, so I reworded it with a short sentence on vacuum and he accepted the change.

The code blocks highlighted properly in both themes. One SQL block was wide and scrolled on narrow screens, which is fine, but I shortened a comment so the key line is visible without scrolling.

Still open: a closing section about the cost of indexes on writes, for which I will measure insert speed with and without the indexes.

summary: Measured insert cost for the index post, with a benchmark of one, three and five indexes, and wrote the findings into the post's closing section with the user.
body:
The post lacked the downside of indexes, so I wrote a benchmark script that inserts 200,000 rows in batches of 1,000 into the orders table with a varying number of indexes.

With no secondary indexes the insert took about 4.1 seconds. With one index it was 5.0, with three 7.6 and with five 11.2 seconds. So each added index cost roughly 15 to 20 percent over the baseline in this setup. The partial index added much less than the full ones, because most new rows are not pending and never enter it.

I ran the benchmark three times and took the median. The spread was under 6 percent, which I noted in the text so nobody reads the numbers as precise. The machine was the user's laptop with a local Postgres, and the post says so.

I also checked a claim he wanted to make about HOT updates. It is true only when the updated column is not indexed, and our test confirmed that updating a non-indexed column kept the index size unchanged while updating an indexed one grew it. I added one sentence on it with the measured numbers.

The user wrote the closing section from these results and I edited it for length. The table of insert times is formatted as Markdown and renders fine in both themes. The post is now complete and awaits a final read. I committed the benchmark script next to the other example scripts and listed the command in a comment.

summary: Published the Postgres index post and verified the page, feed entry and related posts block, which now lists the three Postgres posts in the right order.
body:
After the user's final read I set the published date and turned off draft. The build was clean, the link checker found nothing, and the new alt text check passed since both plan screenshots had descriptions.

On the live site the related posts block at the end showed the EXPLAIN post and the new one, as intended. The feed lists the post first, the sitemap once. The code blocks render in both themes.

One detail: the title was 74 characters, which got cut in the social preview. The user shortened it by a few words and I redeployed.

summary: Looked into a reader report that code blocks overflowed the page on a small phone and fixed it with a min-width rule on the prose container.
body:
A reader wrote that the index post was hard to read on a narrow phone: the page scrolled sideways. I reproduced it in the browser's device mode at 320 pixels wide.

The cause was the insert-time table, which was wider than the viewport and pushed the whole layout. Code blocks already scroll inside their own box. Tables had no such wrapper, since no earlier post had a wide one.

I added a small remark plugin that wraps tables in a div with overflow-x set to auto, and gave it a faint shadow edge as a scroll hint. The prose container also got a min-width of zero, which a flex parent needed so children could shrink.

I then checked every post that has a table. There are five, and all fit or scroll inside their box now. Dark mode looked right too. The build output and image sizes are otherwise unchanged. I replied to nothing myself; the user will answer the reader.

summary: Started a post about the AI SDK with the user by reviewing his streaming chat example and finding it depended on an old API shape that has since changed.
body:
The user wants a post on streaming responses with the AI SDK. He has a small example app from some time ago, so I first checked whether it still runs.

It did not. After installing the current version, the build failed because the helper he used to turn a model stream into a response had been renamed, and the message format for chat history was different. I updated the example to the current calls and ran it against a stubbed model so the output is deterministic.

The stub streams tokens with small delays, which lets the post show the timing of the first token and of the full response without paying for a real model each time. In the example the first token arrives at about 300 ms in the stub and the stream ends at 2.1 seconds, and I made clear in the notes that these are simulated values.

The outline now has four parts: the basic stream, rendering partial text in the browser, handling errors halfway through a stream, and cancelling on the client. I wrote the code for the first two and the user will do the prose.

I put the example in a folder beside the post and pinned the SDK version in its package file so the post stays reproducible. The draft is unpublished.

summary: Added the error-handling and cancellation examples to the AI SDK draft and found that an aborted request left the server stream running until the stub finished.
body:
The next two parts of the AI SDK post needed working code. For errors halfway through a stream I made the stub fail after the fifth token and checked what the client shows. The default was a half sentence with no signal, so the example now catches the error and appends a visible note.

For cancellation I added a stop button that aborts the fetch. In the browser the request ended at once, but the server log showed the stub kept producing tokens for another 1.5 seconds. The cause was that the server handler never passed the request's abort signal to the stream. With the signal passed through, the server stopped within about 50 ms of the abort.

This is a useful point for the post, since real models would keep billing for tokens nobody reads. I wrote it into the outline as a short section with the before and after log lines.

I ran the example three times in a row to check that the results are stable. The tests I wrote for the stub, four small ones, pass. The user will draft the text next.

summary: Reviewed the user's AI SDK draft, correcting a timing claim and a code block that no longer matched the example, and flagged one sentence about pricing for him to verify.
body:
The user finished a full draft and I checked it against the example folder.

The text said the first token arrives in about half a second, but the stub run shows 300 ms. Since the numbers are simulated I also added a sentence saying so, otherwise a reader could take them as model latency. One code block in the cancellation section still showed the version without the abort signal, so it contradicted the paragraph below it. I replaced it with the real file contents.

The import lines in two blocks used the old helper name, which would fail if copied. I fixed them and ran each snippet's imports against the pinned version.

A sentence claimed that a certain model costs a given amount per million tokens. I cannot verify prices from the repository and they change often, so I marked it with a comment for the user and suggested removing the number and linking the provider page instead.

The layout is fine. The post has six code blocks, all highlighted. One is wide, and I checked that it scrolls on a phone width. The reading time shown by the theme is nine minutes.

Remaining work is the pricing decision and one more read by the user. I committed my edits to the draft and left it unpublished.

summary: Published the AI SDK post and then fixed a broken code sandbox link and a feed problem where the example folder was being picked up as a post.
body:
The user decided to drop the price and link the provider page. I applied that, turned off draft and set the date.

The build produced a surprise: the feed contained an extra entry titled after the example folder's README. The content collection glob was matching every Markdown file under the posts directory, including the README in the example subfolder. The drafts filter did not apply because the README has no front matter. I changed the glob to match only the post files named index or the top-level files, and added an ignore for folders called examples.

After the change the feed has the expected entries, and the sitemap also lost a stray page at an odd path. I checked that the old posts that have their own folders for images still load.

The link checker then flagged an external link to a sandbox the user had mentioned, which returned a not found response. He had deleted it. We replaced it with a link to the example folder in the repository.

I also looked at the page on a phone and in dark mode. Code highlighting is right, and the stop-button screenshot has a white background that the dark mode softening handles well.

Last, I wrote a small test for the content glob so a README in a post folder cannot become a page again. It builds a temporary collection and checks the entries. It passes. The user will share the post tomorrow.

summary: Looked into why syntax highlighting was slow in the build after the posts with long code blocks, and cut the build time by caching the highlighter instance.
body:
The build had crept up to about 48 seconds. I profiled it and found that most extra time was in code highlighting: the Markdown pipeline created a new highlighter for every post and reloaded the language grammars each time.

I measured first. Of the 48 seconds, roughly 17 went to highlighting. The three newest posts have long SQL and TypeScript blocks, which made it more visible than before.

The fix was to create the highlighter once at module level and reuse it, loading only the languages the posts actually use: sql, ts, bash, json, yaml and a few others. The list comes from a quick scan of the fence tags in all posts. A post that uses an unlisted language would fall back to plain text, so I added a build check that fails with the post name and the language when a fence tag is not loaded.

After the change the build took 33 seconds, and highlighting about 3. I compared the HTML of every post before and after with a diff and found no change in the code markup. The dual theme colors are identical.

I also checked the dev server, where hot reload of a post with code now takes about a second instead of four.

One caveat is that the cached instance holds memory for the entire build, about 40 MB more, which is no problem on the Netlify builder. I noted the change in the README section on checks. Nothing else was touched, and I left the image step for another day since it is already limited by the size script.

summary: Investigated the comment form spam that got through after a new wave of submissions and strengthened the filter with a time check and a link count, with no false positives on the stored real comments.
body:
The user reported four spam comments in two days, all with several links and generic praise. The existing filter only used a hidden honeypot field, and these submissions filled in nothing there, so they passed.

I looked at the function logs of the last weeks. The spam submissions share three traits: they arrive within one second of the form being loaded, they carry three or more links, and the name field is a URL. Real comments, which I took from the stored data, took at least eight seconds to write and none had more than one link.

I added three rules to the function. First, the form now includes a signed timestamp in a hidden field and the function rejects a submission younger than three seconds. Second, comments with more than two links are held for review instead of posted. Third, a name that looks like a URL is rejected. The rejections return the same thank-you page, so a bot learns nothing from the response.

To check for false positives I replayed all 63 stored real comments through the new rules. None was blocked or held. I also replayed the four spam samples and all four were caught, three by the timestamp and one by the link count.

I wrote six new function tests, one per rule and a few combinations. With the existing eleven tests there are seventeen, all passing. The signed timestamp uses a secret from the Netlify environment, so I added it there and documented the variable in the README. A missing secret makes the function fail closed, with a clear log line.

The form without JavaScript still works, since the timestamp is a plain hidden field rendered at build time. Wait, rendered at build time would make it stale, so I checked that: the field is filled by the function that serves the form page, not at build. I confirmed with a test page loaded twice that shows different values.

I will watch the logs in a few days and tell the user the counts of held and rejected submissions.

summary: Checked the comment filter logs after the first evening and found one held legitimate comment with two links, so the threshold stays but the review email now shows the reason.
body:
A few hours after the deploy I looked at the function logs. Nine submissions came in: six rejected by the timestamp rule, two held for links, and one posted normally.

Of the two held, one was spam and one was a real reader who linked to two related articles and the user's own post. The rule is more than two links, so a third link in a signature tipped it over. I did not loosen the threshold, since the spam wave used four to six links, but a review message that does not say why is hard to act on.

The notification now includes the reason, such as held: 3 links, and a direct link to approve. I added a test for the message text. The user approved the real comment from the email.

No other changes were needed. I will check again after the weekend.

summary: Wrote an upgrade plan for the pending Tailwind major version with the user, listing which prose styles and config would need changes, and decided again to wait.
body:
The user asked whether it is time for the Tailwind major update. I tried it in a scratch copy of the repository without committing anything.

The automatic migration tool changed the config format and the import in the main stylesheet, and the build then ran. Visual comparison against the current screenshots showed differences in seven places: the prose typography for lists, the spacing of blockquotes, the dark palette variables for links, and the default border color, which changed and affected the comment form.

Our theme overrides prose styles heavily, so each difference needs a manual check across post types. I estimated half a day of work for around ten changes and no visible benefit for readers, since the site is static and the CSS size is already 14 KB.

The build time did improve a little, from 33 seconds to about 29. That alone is not a reason to take the risk.

The decision is to stay on the current version and recheck when a security fix or an Astro requirement forces it. I wrote the findings, with the seven differences listed, into the repository notes file so a later upgrade starts from there. The scratch copy was deleted and the working tree is clean.

summary: Started a post about idempotent job handlers with the user and built a small example with a duplicate-delivery test that exposes a double charge.
body:
The user wants a follow-up to the backpressure post about handling the same job twice. We agreed on a worked example: a handler that charges an order and gets the same message delivered two times.

I wrote the example in an examples folder next to the draft, using an in-memory store so it runs without a database. The naive handler reads the order, calls a fake payment function and marks the order paid. A test that delivers the message twice, with a small delay in the payment function, produced two charges. When both deliveries run concurrently, both pass the check before either marks the order paid.

I then wrote two fixes. The first stores an idempotency key per order and does an atomic insert before calling the payment function. A second delivery sees the key and returns the earlier result. The second fix uses a conditional update on the order status so only one delivery wins the transition.

All three variants have tests. The naive one fails on purpose and is marked as expected to fail, so the post can show its output. The two fixed variants pass with 100 concurrent deliveries of the same message, which ran in about 40 ms.

While doing this I found a subtle issue in the first fix: if the payment call fails after the key is stored, the key blocks every later retry. The post should cover that. I added a variant that stores the key with a status and lets a failed attempt be retried, and a test for it.

The outline has five sections: the failure, the key approach, the conditional update, the failed-attempt problem, and when to use which. The test outputs are saved as text files for quoting.

The user will start the prose tomorrow. The draft is marked draft and the example folder is excluded from the content glob, which I verified with the build.

summary: Reviewed the user's idempotent handlers draft, fixing a wrong test output, a mislabeled code block and a claim that the conditional update needs a transaction.
body:
The user wrote the whole draft over the evening and asked for a careful review of the code and claims.

The pasted output of the naive test showed two charges, but a copy of an earlier run had three, which cannot happen with two deliveries. I replaced it with the saved file. One code block was labeled as the key approach but contained the conditional update version, so the text under it described the wrong code. I swapped the block and checked every other label against the file names.

A sentence said the conditional update only works inside a transaction. I tested it: a single update statement with a where clause on the status is atomic on its own, and the example with 100 concurrent deliveries confirms one winner. A transaction is needed only if more than one statement must succeed together. I reworded the sentence and added the distinction.

The section on failed attempts was the strongest, and I only fixed a typo in the status names. The closing guidance is sound, though I suggested adding that both approaches protect only the effect inside your own store; a payment provider needs its own idempotency key passed along. The user liked this and wrote a short paragraph about it.

Technical checks: all six code blocks highlight, the one with long lines scrolls inside its box, the front matter validates against the schema, and the tags match existing ones. The link checker found no broken links. The reading time is eleven minutes.

The post has one image, a diagram of two deliveries racing, drawn as SVG by the user. I converted it to PNG at twice the display size and wrote alt text that describes the sequence in words. Dark mode softening makes the white background fine.

Remaining: a title decision. He is choosing between two, and will publish tomorrow.

summary: Published the idempotent handlers post under the shorter title and checked the live page, feed and the related posts block.
body:
The user chose the shorter title, which fits the social preview without cutting. I set the date and removed the draft flag, then built.

The build was clean and the checks passed, including the alt text check and the fence language check. After deploy I opened the live page in both themes and on a phone width. The code blocks and the diagram looked right.

The feed shows the post first with absolute image URLs. The related posts block now links the backpressure post, which shares the queues tag. The sitemap lists the page once. Nothing needed fixing.

summary: Answered the user's question whether old posts still get readers' clicks from the redirect list, by checking the redirect file against current routes and finding two dead targets.
body:
The user asked if the redirects from the old generator still point to existing pages. I parsed the redirects file and requested every target against a local build.

Of 58 rules, 56 resolve to a live page. Two point to a path that was renamed when the user changed a post slug last year, and they return not found. Both belong to posts about queues.

I fixed the two targets to the new slugs and added a script that checks all redirect targets against the built output. It fails the deploy preview if a target is missing. I ran it, and it passes now.

I did not remove any rule, since readers may still arrive from old links.

summary: Updated Astro and the image package to their latest minors, found that a changed default shifted the image quality setting, and set it explicitly so file sizes stay the same.
body:
A routine update of Astro, Tailwind patch versions and the image optimization package went in today. The install and build worked, but comparing the output with the previous build showed that the WebP files were about 12 percent larger.

The release notes of the image package mention a new default quality value, higher than before. Our config never set it, so we silently got the new default. I set the quality explicitly to the old value, 80, in the image config.

After that, the sizes matched the previous build to within a few bytes for all 96 generated images. I checked this with a script that lists file sizes before and after and prints the differences.

The feed, sitemap and HTML are unchanged by diff, and the build takes 31 seconds. The Tailwind major version stays postponed as decided. I noted the explicit quality setting in the README image section so it does not drift again.

summary: Began a draft about caching strategies for a small API, building the examples with a local test server and measuring hit rates of three simple cache approaches.
body:
The user's next topic is caching in front of a small API. He asked for examples that show real effects, not just advice, so I built a test server with an endpoint that takes about 200 ms to answer and a client that replays a realistic request mix.

The request mix follows a skewed pattern: a small share of keys gets most of the traffic. I generated 50,000 requests over 2,000 keys with that skew.

I tried three approaches. With no cache every request took about 200 ms. With a plain in-process map without limits the hit rate reached 97 percent but memory grew with every key. With a bounded least-recently-used cache of 200 entries the hit rate was 81 percent, and with 500 entries it was 91 percent. The median latency fell from 200 ms to 1 ms for hits.

I also tested a time-to-live of 30 seconds against stale data. When the underlying value changed every 10 seconds, about a third of responses were stale, and I counted them in the client. This will make a good section about the cost of staleness.

One more case is a cache stampede: when a hot key expires, 50 concurrent requests all go to the backend. I added a version that lets one request refill while the others wait, and the backend saw one call instead of 50 in the test.

All scripts are in the examples folder next to the draft and write their results to text files. I made two charts from the hit rate numbers, hit rate by cache size and latency distribution, as PNG with alt text and dark-mode friendly colors.

The outline has five parts: why cache, bounded versus unbounded, staleness, stampedes and what to measure. The user will write the text next. The draft is unpublished, and the build with the new example folder is clean.

summary: Reviewed the user's caching draft, fixing hit-rate numbers that did not match the saved results and a stampede snippet missing its lock release on error.
body:
The user wrote the draft in two sittings and asked for a review before he reads it again.

The text quoted a hit rate of 85 percent for the 200-entry cache, but the saved result says 81. It also gave 92 for the 500-entry cache where the file says 91. I corrected both and checked every other number in the post against the output files. The latency claim of 1 ms for hits was correct.

The stampede snippet had a real bug. It takes a lock for the refill but only releases it after the backend call succeeds. If the backend throws, the lock stays held and every later request for that key waits forever. My example code used a try and finally, but the draft's shortened version dropped it. I restored the finally block and mentioned the failure mode in one sentence, since readers copy short snippets.

I also found a heading that duplicated another one, which broke the contents anchor, and renamed it. One chart caption said hit rate by size while the axis label said by entries, so I made them consistent.

The staleness section claimed that a time-to-live of 30 seconds meant data is at most 30 seconds old. That holds only for a cache that refills on a miss. Our example serves entries until they expire, so that is true there, but with the stampede variant waiting readers can get slightly older data. I added a short qualifier.

Checks: front matter validates, the language fences are loaded, the alt text check passes, and the two charts are optimized to small WebP files. The link checker is clean. The post reads at ten minutes.

Open: the user wants to cut the section on what to measure down to a short list. He will do that and publish after one more read.

summary: Finished the caching post's last measurements by rerunning the three cache approaches with a warm start, and the stampede lock now holds under 200 parallel requests.
body:
The caching draft was reviewed two days ago, and the user asked for one more check before he does his final edits. I reran the local test server with the three cache approaches: a plain time-to-live cache, a size-bounded cache, and a cache with a refresh before expiry. This time each run started with a warm cache, because the first runs had mixed cold-start misses into the hit rates.

The warm numbers moved the hit rates by one to three points, which is small but visible. The plain time-to-live cache ended at 82 percent, the bounded cache at 77 percent, and the refresh-before-expiry cache at 91 percent. I saved the new output as a file next to the old results so the post can name which run it quotes.

I then tested the stampede snippet that got its lock release fixed last week. With 200 parallel requests on one expired key, the backend was called once, and the other requests waited and received the same value. I also forced the loader to throw, and the lock was released, so the next request retried cleanly instead of hanging.

One gap remained. If the loader is very slow, waiting requests pile up without a limit, and the post does not say so. I wrote a short note for the user suggesting one sentence about a wait timeout. I did not change the text myself, because he writes the posts.

I also updated the two numbers in the results table of the draft to the warm-start values and left a comment at each place. The chart still needs to be redrawn from the new file, and I put that on the list for the next session.

summary: Looked into why the comment form showed an error after submit on slow connections and found the function timeout was shorter than the spam filter's time check allowed.
body:
A reader wrote to the user that the comment form showed an error message after sending, although the comment later appeared in the review email. I tried to reproduce it with the browser's network throttling set to a slow connection. After the third try the form showed the same error, so the report was real.

The form posts to the small serverless function, which runs the spam filter and then sends the review email. I read the function log for the failing runs. Each of them ended with a timeout message after ten seconds, and the email had been sent just before the end.

The cause was a call order problem. The function waited for the email service to confirm before it answered the browser. On a slow day of the email service, the confirmation took eight to nine seconds, and with the cold start of the function the total went over the limit. The browser then got a gateway error even though the work was done.

I changed the function so that it validates the input, runs the filter and stores the comment first, and then answers the browser at once. The email is sent after that, and a failure of the email is only logged. I kept the time check of the filter as it was, since it compares timestamps from the form and does not depend on the speed of the function.

I tested the change locally with a fake email service that waits twelve seconds. The form now answered in under one second with the success message. I also tested a submission with two links, which was still held for review with the reason shown, and a submission that was too fast, which was still rejected.

One open point is that a failed email is now only a log line. If the service is down for a long time, comments would wait unseen. I suggested to the user a small daily summary of held comments as a later step. He said he would think about it, and for now the fix is deployed and the form works on the throttled connection.

summary: Published the caching post after the user's final edits and fixed a chart that was served at full size instead of the optimized WebP.
body:
The user made his last edits this afternoon and asked me to publish. I set draft to false, checked the front matter against the schema, and ran the build, which passed without warnings.

On the built page the hit-rate chart was 1.4 MB. The component was importing it through a plain path string in the Markdown rather than through the image pipeline, so the optimizer never touched it. I moved both charts next to the post and referenced them relatively, and the build now emits WebP versions at 800 and 1600 pixels wide. The larger one is 96 KB.

I also wrote alt text for both charts that states what the chart shows, not only its title. The feed entry shows the post at the top with the correct published date, and the related posts block lists the two earlier API-related posts. The live page loaded after the deploy and the sandbox link works.

Nothing is pending on this post.

summary: Wrote the user's requested daily held-comments summary as a small scheduled function, tested it with stored comments, and left it ready for his decision to enable.
body:
Last week the comment form fix made email failures only a log line, and I suggested a daily summary of held comments. The user answered that he wants it, but only if it stays small. I built it as a scheduled function on the same hosting, with no new service and no new dependency.

The function reads the stored comments that are still in the held state and groups them by the reason the filter gave. The reasons are the link count, the time check and the review of new authors. It then builds a plain text message with one line per comment, showing the first sixty characters, the reason and how long it has waited. If nothing is held, it sends nothing at all, so the user does not get empty mail.

I tested it against the stored comments from the filter work in the earlier weeks. Out of 64 stored items, four were in the held state, and the message listed exactly these four with the right reasons. I also tested the empty case by marking all of them as handled, and the function ended without sending.

The schedule needed a decision. I set it to run once a day in the morning, because a comment that waits a full day is acceptable for a personal blog. The user can change the time in the config file, and I wrote a comment at that line.

There was one problem on the way. The function first sent the message even when the email service failed, and the failure was swallowed without a trace. I made it log the error with the number of held comments, so a silent failure leaves a visible line in the function log.

I also added a short section to the repository notes that describes the function, its schedule and how to run it by hand. It is not enabled in production yet. I left the schedule line commented out and told the user that removing the comment character is the only step left. He will enable it after he has read the sample message I pasted into the notes.

summary: Collected the comments on the backpressure post and grouped eleven questions into three themes, mostly about bounded queues versus load shedding, for the user's follow-up post.
body:
The user wants to write a follow-up to the backpressure post and asked what readers raised. I read the stored comments for that post from the comment function's storage, including the ones that were held and later approved.

There were 14 comments, of which 11 contained a real question. I grouped them into three themes. Five asked when to drop work rather than block producers, which the post only touches in one paragraph. Four asked how to pick the queue bound, and whether a fixed number is good enough. Two asked about behavior with several consumers and uneven job sizes.

I wrote the themes into a notes file, notes/backpressure-followup.md, with the comment text quoted briefly and no names or email addresses. That file is not in the content folder, so it does not get built.

I also noticed that two commenters pointed out the same small mistake in the first post: a chart label said 'jobs per minute' where the data is per second. I checked the saved simulation output and they are right. I fixed the label in the chart source and regenerated the PNG, and the build is clean. The user should add a short correction note to the post if he wants one, and I left that sentence for him to write.

summary: Regenerated the corrected backpressure chart and checked that the post and the feed use the new image without a stale cached copy.
body:
After fixing the chart label yesterday I wanted to be sure the corrected image really reaches readers. I rebuilt the site and looked at the generated file names. The optimizer hashes the content, so the new image has a new name and old copies cannot be served from the browser cache.

I opened the built page and found the corrected label 'jobs per second' in both the 800 and 1600 pixel versions. The feed does not embed the chart, so nothing changes there.

One leftover: the Open Graph image for this post was a separate copy of the old chart in the public folder. I replaced it with the new PNG at the same size. The user has not yet decided about a correction note and said he would add one when he works on the follow-up.

summary: Began the follow-up post on load shedding by building a small simulation with a bounded queue that drops the oldest job, and saved first results showing 31 percent fewer late jobs.
body:
The user decided on a follow-up about when to drop work. We started with the simulation, since the first post relied on one too. I copied the earlier simulation into examples/shedding and added three policies: block producers, drop the newest job, and drop the oldest job.

The load pattern is a burst of 3x the consumer rate for 20 seconds followed by normal load. The queue bound is 200. A job counts as late if it finishes more than 5 seconds after it was submitted.

First results, saved to results/shedding-1.json:
- blocking producers: 0 dropped, 38 percent late
- drop newest: 9 percent dropped, 27 percent late
- drop oldest: 9 percent dropped, 26 percent late

The gap between the policies was smaller than I expected. The user's old notes suggested dropping the oldest would be much better. I suspect that the difference only shows when jobs have a deadline after which they are worthless, which is not modeled yet. Next step is adding a deadline field so that stale jobs are skipped by the consumer, then rerunning with several seeds.

summary: Added job deadlines to the shedding simulation and found that with a 5 second deadline dropping the oldest wastes 40 percent less consumer work than dropping the newest.
body:
I extended the simulation so every job carries a deadline, and the consumer skips a job that is already past it. Wasted work is counted as consumer time spent on jobs that finished late.

I ran 20 seeds per policy. With a 5 second deadline, drop newest wasted 22 percent of consumer time and drop oldest wasted 13 percent, about 40 percent less. Blocking producers wasted 35 percent. The spread between seeds was small, under 2 points, so the ordering is stable.

This explains the surprising earlier result: without a deadline the policies look alike, and with one the choice matters. That is a good central point for the post. I saved the numbers to results/shedding-2.json and a table to the notes file. Next is a rough outline for the user.

summary: Wrote an outline for the load shedding post with the user, with four sections and the simulation results mapped to each one, and flagged one claim in his notes that the data does not support.
body:
The user and I worked out the outline. The four sections are: why a bound alone is not enough, the three policies, the effect of deadlines, and how to choose the bound.

I mapped each saved result to a section so every number in the text has a source file. The deadline table goes into the third section, and the first section reuses a chart from the earlier post.

One claim in the user's old notes said that drop oldest is always better. The data does not support this. When jobs have no deadline, the two drop policies were within one point of each other. When jobs are idempotent and a client retries, dropping the newest can even be better, because the client's retry arrives anyway. I suggested he word it as 'better when jobs expire', and he agreed.

The last section needs one more experiment, because the notes only describe the choice of the bound by feel. I will run the simulation with bounds of 50, 200 and 800 next.

summary: Ran the queue bound experiment with 50, 200 and 800 and found that the larger bound only added waiting time without reducing drops during a 20 second burst.
body:
For the last section I ran the shedding simulation with bounds of 50, 200 and 800, using drop oldest and a 5 second deadline, 20 seeds each.

At a bound of 50, 14 percent of jobs were dropped and the median wait was 0.4 seconds. At 200, 9 percent were dropped and the median wait was 1.6 seconds. At 800, 8 percent were dropped and the median wait was 4.1 seconds, which is close to the deadline, so many jobs there were accepted only to expire.

The lesson is that a large bound hides overload by converting drops into late work. A useful rule is to size the bound so that a full queue drains in well under the deadline. With a consumer rate of 100 jobs per second, 200 jobs take 2 seconds, which fits a 5 second deadline. Results are in results/shedding-3.json. I will draw the chart after the user decides which of the three numbers he wants to show.

summary: Drew the wait time versus bound chart for the shedding post as a PNG with a WebP version in the build, and wrote its alt text.
body:
The user chose to show all three bounds, so I made one chart with the bound on the x axis, drop rate as bars and median wait as a line. It was drawn from results/shedding-3.json with the same plotting script as the earlier charts, so the fonts and colors match.

The PNG is 1600 pixels wide. I placed it next to the draft and referenced it relatively so that the build produces the optimized sizes. The 800 pixel WebP is 38 KB.

Alt text: 'Bars show the drop rate at queue bounds 50, 200 and 800, falling from 14 to 8 percent, and a line shows median wait rising from 0.4 to 4.1 seconds.' I also added a caption that mentions the 5 second deadline. The chart reads well on a narrow phone because the labels are large, which I checked with the responsive view in the browser.

The user has the draft text left to write.

summary: Reviewed the user's first full draft of the load shedding post and corrected two figures, a wrongly named policy in one code block, and a claim about blocking producers.
body:
The user finished a full draft and asked me to check it. I compared all numbers with results/shedding-1 to 3.

Two figures were wrong. The text said drop oldest wasted 15 percent of consumer time, but the saved result is 13. It also said the bound of 800 gave a median wait of 4.7 seconds, where the data says 4.1. I fixed both.

In the code block for the second policy, the function was named dropNewest but its body removed the head of the queue, which is the oldest job. This was from a copy and paste of the example. I used the actual file, ran it, and renamed the function in the post to dropOldest.

The text also said that blocking producers 'always causes timeouts upstream'. In the simulation, producers blocked and 38 percent of jobs were late, but not all failed. I proposed 'often causes' and he took it.

The structure is good and the intro is strong. I did not change his style. Left to do: a final read for links and the front matter.

summary: Checked the load shedding draft's links and front matter before publication and fixed a link to the first backpressure post that pointed at its old path.
body:
Early check before the user's final edits. I ran the link checker script over the draft and over the built page.

One internal link pointed to /blog/queue-backpressure, which is the path from before the post was renamed. The redirect file catches it, but a redirect inside the site is unnecessary, so I changed the link to the current path. The other five links, including two external ones to the library docs, were fine.

Front matter: the description was 212 characters, longer than the 160 we use for search snippets, so I shortened it and showed him the new text. Tags were consistent with the earlier posts, with 'queues' and 'backpressure'. The updated field is not set, as intended for a new post.

The build passed. He plans to publish this evening or tomorrow.

summary: Published the load shedding post and checked the page, the feed entry, and the related posts block, which now links the two queue posts.
body:
The user made his last edits and I published the post. I set draft to false and built the site locally first, with no warnings.

After the deploy I opened the live page. The chart loads as WebP and the alt text is present. The code blocks do not overflow on a narrow viewport, which was a problem some time ago and is now fixed by the prose rule.

The feed lists the post first with the right published date. The related posts block shows the earlier backpressure post and the idempotent handlers post, which seems right. The sitemap includes the new URL and no redirected paths.

The user also added a short correction note at the top of the first backpressure post about the per-second label, which I checked in the built page. I did not find anything else to fix, and no issues remain.

summary: Looked into a reader report of a broken chart on the shedding post and found that the Open Graph image path was missing, so shared links showed no preview.
body:
A reader wrote to the user that the post showed no image when shared in a chat app. I checked the built page head.

The og:image tag was present but pointed to /images/shedding-og.png, a file that I never created, since the layout builds that path from the slug. The earlier posts have their images in public/images, put there by hand. For this post the file was simply missing, and the server returned the 404 page.

I made the image from the chart at 1200 by 630 pixels as a PNG and put it at the expected path. Then I thought about how to prevent this. I added a check to the build script that fails when a post's og image path does not exist in public. When I ran it over all posts, it found one more: a post from the migration period with a missing image. I pointed that one to the default site image.

After the deploy I tested the URL with curl and got a 200 with content-type image/png. Chat apps cache previews for a while, so the reader may need to wait. The user will tell the reader.

summary: Updated the dependencies to their latest minor versions and found that a Tailwind typography patch changed the spacing of list items in posts, which I pinned back.
body:
I ran the routine dependency update, with Tailwind staying on its current major version as decided before. The Astro, image, RSS and syntax highlighting packages went up by minor or patch versions.

The build passed, but comparing screenshots of three posts I saw that lists had more space between items. The cause was a patch release of the typography plugin that changed the margin on list items inside prose. This is not a bug in the plugin but a different default.

I could have adapted the CSS, but the spacing is pleasant in the old version and the posts have many lists. I pinned the plugin to the previous patch version with an exact version number and wrote a comment in package.json notes. The screenshots matched again.

The feed output and image file sizes did not change. The audit shows no known vulnerabilities. I will look at the plugin again when the Tailwind major update is planned.

summary: Started a draft about a homelab backup setup with the user, listing his notes and checking the restore commands against a test directory.
body:
The user wants to write about how he backs up his home server. We began with his notes, which are a text file of shell commands and a rough list of what is backed up: photos, a database dump, and configuration files.

Before building a post on commands I wanted to know that they work. I made a test directory with a few hundred small files and a dump, and ran the backup commands from the notes against a local folder as the target.

The backup itself worked, but the restore step in the notes had a mistake: it restored into the current directory without a target flag, which would overwrite files in place. I found it because my test restore replaced the sample files. In the draft it now uses an explicit target path and a dry run first.

The notes also mention a retention rule that keeps 7 daily and 4 weekly snapshots, but the script has 7 daily and 3 weekly. I asked the user which is true, and he said four was the intent, so the script needs a fix on his server. That is his machine, so I only noted it.

Next I will write the outline and the test script that the post can quote.

summary: Wrote a restore test script for the backup post that restores a snapshot into a temporary folder and compares checksums, and it passed on 412 files.
body:
For the post I made a script, examples/backup/verify.sh, that does what the user said readers should do: restore the latest snapshot into a temporary folder and compare checksums with the source.

It lists files with their hashes on both sides, sorts them and compares with diff. On my test directory with 412 files it reported no differences. I then changed one file after the backup and the script reported exactly that file, so it detects a difference and does not only pass.

Two details were needed. Files that change during the backup, such as the database file, produce false differences, so the script takes an exclude list and the post explains that a dump should be tested instead. And file timestamps differ after a restore on some filesystems, so only content hashes are compared.

The script is 24 lines. I saved sample output for the post. The user wants to show it as the main idea: a backup is not a backup before it has been restored once.

summary: Reviewed the user's backup post draft and corrected a wrong retention number, an unsafe restore command and a sentence claiming that checksums prove the data is correct.
body:
The user wrote the whole backup draft and I reviewed it against the test script and the notes.

The retention rule in the text said three weekly snapshots, while the intent and the later fix on his server say four. I changed it to four. One restore command was still the old form without a target path, from an early part of the draft, and I replaced it with the safe one.

A sentence said that matching checksums prove the data is correct. They prove that the restore equals the source at the time of the backup, not that the source was not already corrupt. I suggested a softer wording and added a line about checking the application, for example opening a few photos.

I also found that a code block was labeled bash but contained a config file excerpt, so I relabeled it as ini. The text on offsite copies was missing a mention of encryption, and he said he would add a paragraph. I did not write it, since the choices are his.

summary: Published the homelab backup post and fixed the code highlighting for the ini block, which the highlighter did not know as a language alias.
body:
The user finished the encryption paragraph and I published the post late in the evening.

On the built page the ini block had no colors. The highlighter config lists the languages it loads, to keep the build fast, and ini was not on the list. I added it, and the build time did not noticeably change, about 14 seconds before and after.

The feed contains the post and the page loads normally. The related posts block shows no related posts for it, because it is the only post with the tag 'homelab'. That is fine, and I left the empty block hidden as it was designed.

The verify script is linked as a file in the example folder. I checked that the folder is still excluded from the feed, which was a problem earlier. Done.

summary: Looked at the user's idea for a dark mode and found that the existing color classes cover most of the theme, so a toggle needs about a dozen overrides.
body:
The user asked how much work a dark mode would be. I read through the theme to estimate it before suggesting anything.

The layout uses Tailwind color classes in about 30 places and a few fixed hex colors in the CSS for code blocks and the comment form. With the class-based dark variant, most of the classes only need a dark: counterpart. I counted 13 places that need explicit overrides, such as the code block background, the table borders and the form inputs.

Two risks: the syntax highlighter theme is light, so it would need a second theme and a build change, and the charts in older posts are PNGs with white backgrounds that would look like bright boxes. Those cannot be changed without regenerating each chart.

My suggestion was to follow the system setting first and add a toggle later, and to give the charts a light rounded frame. He liked that and asked me to try it.

summary: Built the dark mode that follows the system setting, with a second highlighter theme and framed charts, and checked the home page, a post and the comment form in both modes.
body:
I implemented the dark mode as planned. Tailwind's dark variant is set to media, so it follows the system setting and needs no script.

The 13 places with explicit colors were converted. The layout, the nav, the footer and the prose styles got dark: counterparts, and the typography plugin's invert class is applied in dark mode on the prose container. The pinned plugin version supports this.

For code, I configured the highlighter with two themes and a CSS variable approach, so that no extra build step runs per post. The build time stayed at about 14 seconds, which I measured twice. The comment form inputs had white backgrounds and grey borders that were fixed in the CSS, and I checked the error and success states.

The charts in older posts are PNGs with white backgrounds. I put them in a figure with a light background, padding and a small radius, so they look intentional in dark mode and the page keeps its contrast. The three oldest posts have screenshots, and I looked at them too, which are fine.

I went through the home page, the archive, a long post and the comment form with the browser's emulated dark setting, and also checked the contrast of links and muted text. Two muted texts had a contrast ratio of 3.8 and I brightened them to pass 4.5.

The feed and the build output for the other pages did not change. Not done: a manual toggle. The user wants to use it for a few days first.

summary: Fixed a flash of the wrong color on the archive page in dark mode, caused by a hard-coded white background on the cover image placeholder.
body:
The user noticed that opening the archive page in dark mode briefly showed white rectangles before the cover images appeared. I looked at the markup of the archive cards.

The lazy loaded cover images use a placeholder box with a fixed light grey background so the layout does not jump. That color was a hex value in a small CSS file and I had missed it, as it is not a Tailwind class. In dark mode it is a bright box until the image arrives.

I changed the placeholder to use a theme color variable with a dark counterpart and checked it with the network throttled to slow 3G, which makes the loading state visible. The boxes are now dark and then fade to the image.

I searched the CSS for other hex colors and found two more, a border on the blockquote and the selection color. The blockquote border is fine in both modes, and I adjusted the selection color. No other changes. I then checked the layout shift score of the archive page and it is still 0, as before.

summary: Checked the site after a quiet stretch: build, links, feed and dependencies were all fine, and the only open item is the unpublished caching follow-up idea in the notes.
body:
Nothing urgent came in, so I did a routine health check of the repository. The build passes in about 14 seconds and the link checker found no broken internal or external links.

The feed validates and lists the posts in the right order. The sitemap has no redirected paths. The redirect file still has the two dead targets that I reported earlier, which the user chose to leave until he decides about those old posts.

Dependencies: only patch updates are pending, plus the Tailwind major version, which remains postponed. The typography plugin stays pinned to the exact version.

Open items are the manual dark mode toggle, if he wants one, and the notes file for a possible follow-up about cache invalidation. I wrote them into the state summary in the repository notes. No other work is planned right now.

summary: Started the caching follow-up draft on conditional requests, measuring how ETag and Last-Modified revalidation cut bytes sent by a small test API.
body:
The notes had one open idea, a follow-up to the caching post about conditional requests. I built a small local test server with three endpoints: no validators, ETag only, and Last-Modified only. A script replayed 1,000 requests over 50 resources with a client that kept the validators.

Without validators every request sent the full body, about 4.2 MB in total. With ETag, 71 percent of requests came back as 304 and total bytes fell to 1.3 MB. Last-Modified gave nearly the same result, 69 percent.

The odd part was the weak ETag case. When the server computed the tag from the serialized JSON, key order changed between runs and the hit rate dropped to 12 percent. I fixed the serializer to sort keys and the rate returned to 71 percent. This is probably worth its own section in the post.

Results are saved in experiments/conditional/results.json with the script next to it. Nothing is written in the post yet. Next I will check how the numbers change when resources are updated during the run, since the first run used static data only. I also noted that the test server needs a fixed seed so the user can rerun it and get the same figures.

I did not touch the site code. The draft file exists in the drafts folder with only a title and the three measured tables, and it is marked as draft so it stays out of the build and the feed.

summary: Reran the conditional request test with resources changing mid-run and found ETag revalidation still saved 48 percent of bytes at a 20 percent update rate.
body:
I extended the test server so a random 20 percent of resources changed during the replay, using a fixed seed of 7 so the run repeats. The same 1,000 requests over 50 resources were used as before.

With ETag the 304 share dropped from 71 to 52 percent, and total bytes went from 1.3 MB to 2.2 MB. Compared with the no-validator baseline of 4.2 MB that still saves 48 percent. Last-Modified behaved the same except for one case: two updates within the same second were not noticed, so a client kept a stale body for 3 requests. That is a good concrete example for the post, since one-second resolution is easy to forget.

I added a column for stale responses to the results table. ETag had zero, Last-Modified had 3. The results file was updated and the old static-data results were kept under a separate key.

Next step is to tell the user about the stale case and let him decide whether the post should recommend ETag only. I did not edit the draft text, since he writes the posts.

summary: Reviewed the user's first draft of the conditional requests post, fixing two table figures and an example that sent If-None-Match with the wrong header casing in the code.
body:
The user finished a first draft of the conditional requests post and asked for a review. I compared every number against experiments/conditional/results.json.

Two figures in the second table were off: the stale response count for Last-Modified said 5 where the file says 3, and the bytes for the changing-resource run used the static-data value. Both are corrected in the draft.

The curl example sent the header as If-None-Matched, which would never match. It now reads If-None-Match, and I ran the command against the test server to confirm it returned a 304.

I also flagged a sentence saying ETag always beats Last-Modified. The data shows nearly the same savings, with the only difference being the stale case, so I suggested wording about one-second resolution instead. The user accepted that edit.

Front matter was fine except for a missing description field, which I added as a placeholder for him to rewrite. Left open: a chart for the bytes comparison, which he wants, and a decision on the title.

summary: Drew the bytes-sent comparison chart for the conditional requests post as a PNG with a WebP version, and wrote its alt text.
body:
The user wanted one chart showing total bytes for no validators, Last-Modified and ETag, in both the static and the changing-data runs. I drew it as grouped bars with the plotting script and saved a PNG at 1600 pixels wide.

The build creates the WebP version from the PNG, so I only added the source file to the post's image folder. The WebP came out at 34 KB against 58 KB for the PNG.

The alt text says what the chart shows: bars for three approaches, with ETag at 1.3 MB in the static run and 2.2 MB with changing data, against 4.2 MB without validators. I also checked the chart in dark mode, where the framed style from earlier keeps the white plot background readable.

The chart is referenced in the draft right after the second table.
