summary: Checked the conditional requests draft before publication, fixing a broken link to the caching post and a missing description, and confirmed the build and feed are clean.
body:
Before the user publishes, I ran the pre-publish checks on the draft. The build passed with no warnings, and the link checker found one broken link: the reference to the caching post used the old slug without the trailing path, which returned a 404 from the redirect list.

I corrected the link to the current route. The description field now holds the text the user wrote this evening, 142 characters, within the limit used for previews.

The Open Graph image path, which broke on an earlier post, resolved correctly here. I rendered the page locally and checked the code blocks, both tables and the chart, in light and dark mode.

I also built the feed and confirmed the draft stays out while its draft flag is set. Once he flips the flag, the entry should appear at the top. The one remaining item is his final read of the intro paragraph, which he said he wants to reword.

summary: Published the conditional requests post and checked the live page, the feed entry, the related posts block, and the optimized chart, all of which were correct.
body:
The user flipped the draft flag and pushed, and Netlify finished the deploy in about two minutes. I then checked the live site.

The post page loaded with the right title and description. The chart was served as WebP at the expected size, 34 KB, not the PNG. That was a problem once before, so I looked at the network response specifically.

The feed had the new entry at the top with the full content and an absolute URL for the chart. I validated the feed file and found no errors. The related posts block on the new page lists the caching post and the load shedding post, and the caching post now links back to the new one.

I tested the Open Graph tags with the raw HTML and saw the image path resolved to a 200. The sitemap included the new URL.

I also tried the post on a throttled connection to see whether the lazy loading of the chart caused layout shift. The image has width and height attributes, so nothing jumped.

No comments yet. The comment form on the new page submitted a test entry and it landed in the held list as expected, and I deleted the test entry afterwards. Nothing is left open on this post. The notes file now has the caching idea crossed out.

summary: Investigated why the build time rose from 48 to 71 seconds and traced it to the image optimizer reprocessing unchanged charts because the cache folder was not kept.
body:
The user noticed that deploys felt slower, so I timed local builds. A clean build took 71 seconds, up from the 48 I measured after the last dependency update.

I checked the build log for the slow step. The image step handled 214 images each time, including old charts that had not changed. The cache folder for optimized images was set to a path inside node_modules, which a clean install wipes on Netlify, so every deploy redid everything.

I moved the cache directory to a folder that Netlify keeps between builds and added it to the cache settings. Locally, a second build dropped to 19 seconds.

I then ran a deploy to confirm. The first deploy after the change still took 70 seconds because the cache was empty. The next deploy, with one small text change, took 27 seconds and the log said 211 images came from the cache.

One risk is a stale cache after the quality setting changes. The cache key includes the options, and I tested by changing quality from 80 to 75 and saw all images reprocessed, so this is covered.

I wrote the cache location in the README so it is not lost. Nothing else changed in the site.

summary: Answered the user's question whether any post still uses an image over 300 KB, finding three, all PNG sources whose WebP outputs are under 100 KB.
body:
The user asked if large images are still hurting any page. I listed all source images in the posts folders by size and then compared with the built output.

Three sources are above 300 KB: the queue diagram at 412 KB, the backpressure chart at 336 KB, and the early Postgres index screenshot at 388 KB. All are PNG. In the build, each is served as WebP, with the largest output at 92 KB.

I also checked the sizes that reach the browser on the three pages with the network panel and saw the WebP versions, with sizes matching the build folder.

So no page ships an oversized image. The only cost is repository size, about 1.1 MB for those three. I suggested leaving them, since the user wants the originals kept for editing. He agreed.

summary: Updated dependencies, found that a new syntax highlighter minor renamed the theme option and broke the dark code theme, and fixed the config so both themes render again.
body:
I ran the routine dependency update. Astro stayed the same, but Tailwind, the typography plugin and the highlighter had new minors.

The build passed, yet a post page in dark mode showed code blocks with the light theme. The highlighter release had renamed the option that holds the second theme, and the old name was silently ignored. I found it in the changelog, then changed the config to the new key.

After the change the build produced the dual-theme CSS variables again. I checked three posts with code: the backpressure post, the Postgres index post and the backup post with the ini block. The ini alias fix from before still worked.

The typography plugin changed nothing visible this time. I compared list spacing against screenshots from the last update and it matched the pinned values.

To catch this class of problem, I added a small check script that builds the site and looks for the dark theme variable in the output CSS. It fails the build if it is missing. It runs in about two seconds after a build.

I committed the update, the config change and the check together. Open item: the highlighter has a deprecation warning for another option, which I left because it still works.

summary: Looked at the comment spam filter's recent results and found the held list had 38 entries, 36 spam and 2 real comments caught by the link-count rule.
body:
The user asked how well the spam filter is doing, since he had not looked at held comments in a while. I read the held list from the stored comments.

There were 38 held entries. I read each one. 36 were clearly spam, mostly with several links or the same text in different names. Two were real: one question about queue bounds and one thanks note, each with two links, which the filter holds when a comment has more than one link.

No spam was approved, as far as I could tell from the approved list of 14 comments, which I also read.

I considered raising the link limit to 2. In the held list, 9 spam entries had exactly two links, so that would let some through. I suggested keeping the rule and instead telling the user about the two real ones so he can approve them.

He approved both by hand. I did not change the filter. The daily summary function is still not enabled, and he said he would consider turning it on if the held list kept growing.

summary: Enabled the daily held-comments summary at the user's request after testing it once against the live held list, and set it to send at 8 in the morning.
body:
After the last look at the held list, the user decided to turn on the scheduled summary function. I first ran it once manually against the stored comments to see the output.

The summary listed 3 new held comments with name, first 80 characters and link count. It skipped entries already reported, using a marker stored with each comment. I ran it twice and the second run reported nothing new, which is correct.

I then set the schedule in the function config to 8 in the morning, UTC, and confirmed it in the Netlify function list after the deploy. The email address comes from an environment variable, which the user set himself in the Netlify settings.

One issue came up: with zero new comments the function still sent an empty message. I changed it to send nothing in that case and added a test for it. All 4 tests pass.

The next real check is tomorrow morning, when the first scheduled run should happen. If nothing arrives, the function logs will show whether the schedule or the sending failed.

summary: Checked the first scheduled runs of the summary function, found it sent nothing because the schedule used a cron field the platform rejected, and fixed it.
body:
The user said no summary email had arrived in two days, though there were new held comments. I opened the function logs.

There were no runs at all, so the problem was the schedule, not the sending. The deploy log showed a warning I had missed: the cron expression I wrote had a sixth field for seconds, which the platform does not accept, so it ignored the schedule.

I changed the expression to five fields, 0 8 * * *, redeployed, and the function list showed the schedule. To avoid waiting a day, I triggered the function through the invoke command and it ran correctly. It reported 5 held comments, which arrived by mail within a minute.

I also added a line to the README about the schedule format and the manual invoke command.

The lesson is that the first manual test only proved the code, not the schedule. I added a check to the deploy notes: after changing a schedule, look for a first run in the logs the next day.

Of the 5 held comments, 4 were spam and 1 was a real question on the caching post, which I reported to the user. The next morning's run is the confirmation.

summary: Confirmed the summary function ran on schedule this morning and sent one email with two held comments, so the earlier cron fix works.
body:
I checked the function logs after the user said the email arrived. There was a run at 8 in the morning with exit status ok, and it took 410 ms.

The email listed two held comments, both spam, with link counts of 4 and 6. The marker logic skipped the five comments reported earlier.

I also looked at the run of the day before, which also existed. It sent nothing since no new comments had come in, so the empty-message change works in real use.

No further changes were needed. I removed the note about checking the first run from the open items. The function now needs no attention unless the volume of spam changes.

summary: Looked into the user's idea of adding reading time to post cards and built it as a build-time calculation, adding it to the home page and archive.
body:
The user asked for a reading time on each post card. I computed it at build time from the Markdown body so no client script is needed.

The function strips code blocks and front matter, counts words, and divides by 220 words per minute, rounding up with a minimum of 1 minute. Code blocks were left out because counting them made the backpressure post look like 14 minutes, while the prose alone gives 9.

I added the result in a small helper, used by the post card component and the post header. The archive page and home page now show text like 9 min read in the muted text color. In dark mode the contrast is fine, I measured a ratio of 5.1.

I checked the 21 existing posts. Reading times range from 3 to 12 minutes. The shortest is the redirect post at 3.

The RSS feed was not changed, since feed readers show their own estimate. I built the site, checked the pages in both modes and found no layout change on narrow screens. The user liked it and kept it. One open question is whether the reading time should count tables; for now it does not.

summary: Fixed the reading time helper so a post with a long table no longer under-reports, by counting table cell text as words.
body:
The user noticed the conditional requests post showed 4 minutes, which felt short for a post with three tables. I checked the helper and saw that the code-stripping regex also removed table rows, because it matched lines starting with a pipe.

I narrowed the regex to fenced code blocks and inline code only. Table text now counts as words after the pipes and separator rows are removed.

The post moved from 4 to 6 minutes. Two other posts with tables also went up by one minute. All other posts were unchanged, which I verified by comparing the full list before and after.

I added a test with a short sample containing a table and a code block, and it passes. The change is committed.

summary: Investigated a reader report that the comment form failed on a phone, finding that the hidden time-check field was filled in by the browser's autofill and tripped the spam filter.
body:
The user forwarded a message from a reader who could not post a comment from a phone, getting the generic error. I looked for the cause in the function logs, where one submission around that time was rejected with the reason honeypot filled.

The honeypot field was named website, which some autofill features fill with the user's own site address. The reader's browser had filled it. Real bots fill it too, so the check itself is good, but the name was a poor choice.

I renamed the field to a neutral name, added autocomplete off and a tabindex of -1, and kept it hidden by moving it off screen rather than display none, since some bots skip fields hidden that way. The function accepts both old and new names for a day or two so forms already open in a browser still work.

I tested with a headless browser that fills all fields and it was rejected, and with a normal submission, which passed. I also tried a mobile emulation with autofill-like behavior by filling only visible fields, and it passed.

I told the user to reply to the reader and ask them to try again. The error message shown on rejection is still generic. I suggested a clearer one, such as asking the reader to reload and try again, but did not change the text without the user's wording. The logs will show whether honeypot rejections drop in the coming weeks.

summary: Removed the old honeypot field name from the comment function after a quiet stretch and changed the rejection message to the wording the user chose.
body:
The grace period for the old honeypot name is over, so I removed it from the comment function. The logs showed no submissions using the old name in the last four days.

I also changed the error text. The user chose: Something went wrong with your comment. Please reload the page and try again. It replaces the generic error and is used for the honeypot and the time-check rejections alike, so spammers learn nothing about the reason.

The function tests were updated for the new text and the single field name. All 7 tests pass. I checked the form on the live page after the deploy, and a test comment was held as expected. I deleted it afterwards.

In the logs of the past week there were 2 honeypot rejections, down from about 15 a week, so the rename helped with real autofill cases or the bots changed. I cannot tell which.

summary: Checked the site's accessibility basics on the home page and a post, finding two missing alt texts on old images and a low-contrast link color in dark mode.
body:
The user asked for a quick accessibility look. I ran an automated audit against the built home page, the archive and three posts.

It flagged two images without alt text, both in the old Postgres index post, where the screenshots had empty alt attributes. I wrote descriptions after reading the surrounding text: one for the query plan before the index and one for the plan after, mentioning the change from a sequential scan to an index scan.

The second finding was link color in dark mode. Links in the muted paragraph style had a contrast ratio of 3.8, below the 4.5 target. I lightened the dark link color one step in the Tailwind class and the ratio became 5.6.

The heading order was fine and the comment form fields all had labels. The skip link works.

I rebuilt and ran the audit again, and no errors remained on those pages. Left open: the audit only tested six pages, so older posts may have more missing alt text. I suggested a build-time check for empty alt attributes.

summary: Added a build-time check that fails on images without alt text and used it to find and fix seven more missing descriptions in older posts.
body:
Following the earlier audit, I wrote a small script that scans all Markdown posts for images with empty alt text and runs after the build. It exits with an error and lists the file and line.

On the first run it found seven images in five posts: two in the queue post, three in the Astro migration post and two in the AI SDK post. Most were screenshots with an empty alt.

I wrote alt text for each after opening the images. The migration screenshots show the old site's folder tree, the new content config and the redirect file, so the text names those. For the AI SDK post, the two images are terminal output, so I described the key lines of output rather than the whole screen.

I kept the texts short, between 60 and 120 characters. The user wanted a look at them, and he changed one for the redirect file to be more specific.

The script treats decorative images specially if the alt is explicitly empty with a marker comment, but none needed that. I added the check to the build command so a deploy fails if an image lacks alt.

I tested by removing one alt on purpose and saw the deploy preview fail with the file name. After restoring it the build passed. The check runs in under a second. The README now describes it. Nothing else is open for this topic.

summary: Looked at why the archive page lists two posts in the wrong order and found that both had the same date, so the sort needs a tie-break on the title.
body:
The user saw that two posts from the same day appeared in a different order on the archive than on the home page. I compared the sorting code in both places.

The home page sorts by date and then by slug, while the archive sorted by date only, so the order of equal dates depended on file reading order. That differs between local and Netlify builds.

I moved the sort into one helper that sorts by date descending, then by title, and used it in the home page, the archive, the feed and the related posts block. The feed order is now stable too.

I built twice and compared the output of the archive, and the order was identical. The user confirmed it matched what he expected. Two tests cover the tie case.

summary: Drafted a plan with the user for a post on measuring a small service's tail latency, listing the experiments needed and building the first load test harness.
body:
The user wants a new post about tail latency in a small service and asked me to help plan and measure. We agreed on three questions: how far p99 sits from the median under steady load, what a slow dependency does to it, and whether a timeout helps.

I built a harness with a local test server that has a configurable dependency delay, and a load script that sends requests at a fixed rate of 100 per second for 60 seconds and records each latency. The results go to a CSV file with a summary script for percentiles.

The first run used no delay on the dependency. The median was 3.1 ms, p95 was 6.4 ms and p99 was 14 ms, so the tail was about 4.5 times the median even in the easy case. Part of that was the garbage collector, which I saw in a separate trace as short pauses every few seconds.

The second run made 5 percent of dependency calls take 200 ms. The median stayed at 3.4 ms, but p99 jumped to 212 ms, as expected, and p95 was 198 ms because exactly 5 percent were slow. This gives a clean example of how a small slow share dominates the tail.

I noticed that the load script itself needed to avoid coordinated omission. At first it waited for each response before sending the next, which hid the delay. I changed it to send on a fixed schedule and measure from the intended send time. With the fix the p99 in the slow run rose from 212 to 340 ms, which is a more honest number.

All runs and the scripts are saved in experiments/latency. Next steps are the timeout experiment and an outline with the user. I did not start the draft text.

summary: Ran the timeout experiment for the tail latency post and found a 50 ms timeout cut p99 from 340 to 61 ms while failing the 5 percent of calls that were slow.
body:
I added a timeout option to the test server's dependency call and reran the slow dependency scenario, with 5 percent of calls taking 200 ms and the same fixed-rate schedule as before.

Without a timeout the p99 was 340 ms, as in the last run. With a 100 ms timeout p99 fell to 112 ms. With a 50 ms timeout p99 was 61 ms. In both cases the slow share came back as errors, so 5.0 percent of requests failed at 50 ms against 5.1 at 100 ms.

So a timeout does not remove the slow calls, it turns waiting into failing. That is the main point for the post, and it connects to the load shedding post from earlier.

I also tried a fallback value for a timed out call, which kept the error rate at zero, but the answer was stale. I counted it as a separate row so the post can say what the trade is.

The results are in experiments/latency/results.json and a table is ready to paste. I told the user about the numbers and suggested a chart of latency percentiles by timeout setting. He wants to write the outline next.

summary: Ran the hedged request experiment for the tail latency post: a second request after 40 ms cut p99 from 340 to 88 ms while adding about 9 percent more load.
body:
The tail latency post needed a second technique next to timeouts, so I added hedging to the load test harness built last week. The client sends one request, and if there is no answer after a set delay it sends a second one and takes whichever answer comes first. The test service still has the same shape: most calls take about 12 ms and 5 percent take 300 ms or more.

I ran three hedge delays, 20, 40 and 80 ms, with 20000 calls each at a fixed rate of 200 per second. At 20 ms the p99 fell to 52 ms, but the extra requests were 31 percent of the total, which made the service queue and pushed p50 up from 12 to 19 ms. At 40 ms the p99 was 88 ms and the extra load was 9 percent, with p50 unchanged. At 80 ms the p99 was 141 ms and the extra load was 5 percent.

The result matches what the post will argue: hedging at about the p95 latency is cheap, and hedging earlier pays for the gain with load that makes the tail worse again. Unlike the 50 ms timeout from the earlier run, hedging did not fail any of the slow calls, since the slow ones still finish if the second request is slow too.

The raw numbers are in results/hedge-*.json next to the timeout results, and the harness has a new --hedge-ms flag. One thing I am not sure of yet is whether the two requests are independent in this test. Both go to the same process, so a real slowdown of the whole service would hit both. I noted that as a caveat for the post and as the next experiment: make the slowness depend on a single replica and compare.

summary: Added a second run of the hedging test where slowness is tied to one of two replicas, and p99 improved less than before: 340 to 120 ms at the 40 ms delay.
body:
This was the follow-up to the caveat from the hedging run an hour ago. I changed the test service so that it runs as two instances behind a small round-robin proxy, and one of them gets slow in bursts of about two seconds. This is closer to the case where a request is slow because of where it landed, not because of bad luck inside one process.

With no hedging, p99 was 355 ms. With a 40 ms hedge delay it was 120 ms, compared with 88 ms in the single instance test. The reason is that round-robin sometimes sent the second request to the same slow instance, because the proxy has no memory of where the first one went. I changed the proxy so the hedge always goes to the other instance, and p99 dropped to 64 ms with the same 9 percent extra load.

That difference is worth a section in the post. Hedging only works as well as the independence of the two attempts, and the cheapest way to get independence is to send the second attempt somewhere else.

I also checked that the harness measures latency from the first send, not from the second one. It did, but only by accident of how the timer was started, so I added a test with a fake clock to keep it that way. All of the numbers now sit in results/hedge-replicas.json.

Next is the part of the post about combining a timeout with a hedge, which the user wants as the closing recommendation. I did not start it yet.

summary: Added a second hedging run where the slowness sits on one of two replicas, and p99 improved less than before: 340 to 120 ms at the 40 ms delay.
body:
The first hedging run assumed every call had the same small chance of being slow. Real slowness often comes from one bad node, so the harness got a second mode where one of two replicas is slow. In that mode the slow replica adds a 300 ms stall to about 10 percent of its calls and the other replica stays fast.

I changed the test server in loadtest/server.py to take a --slow-replica flag and start two instances on separate ports. The client picks a replica at random for the first request. The hedged copy goes to the other replica, which is a deliberate choice, because sending it to the same one would hide the effect.

The baseline without hedging gave a p99 of 340 ms, the same as in the earlier run. With a 40 ms hedge delay p99 fell to 120 ms, not the 88 ms seen before. The extra load was about 9 percent again, so the cost did not change while the benefit shrank.

The reason is visible in the traces. When the first request lands on the slow replica and the hedge goes to the fast one, the call finishes in about 45 ms. When the first request lands on the fast replica, no hedge is needed. But a few calls hit the slow replica both times, because the random choice for the hedge was not excluding the first target in an early version of my code. I fixed that and reran the whole sweep.

I also ran delays of 20, 40, 80 and 120 ms. At 20 ms the extra load rose to 21 percent with p99 at 104 ms. At 80 ms the extra load was 4 percent and p99 was 190 ms. The 40 ms setting stayed the best compromise, near the p95 of the fast replica.

Each point is the median of five runs of 20000 calls, and the spread of p99 across runs was under 8 ms. I saved the raw numbers in a CSV next to the first experiment so the chart can use both. For the post, the main point is that hedging helps most when slowness is random and less when it is tied to one node. The user wants that caveat in the text, and the next step is to draft the post around the three experiments.

The text also said hedging costs nothing when the service is healthy. That is not true in the data: the extra load was 9 percent at the 40 ms delay. I changed the sentence to say the cost is small and grows quickly as the delay gets shorter, and pointed to the 31 percent figure at 20 ms.

Two smaller things: the code sample for the hedge did not cancel the slower request, which would leave work running, so I added the cancel call. And the term tail latency was used for p99 in one place and for p99.9 in another, so I suggested saying the percentile each time.

The structure was good. The opening with the one slow call in twenty works, and the order of timeout, hedge and combination follows the experiments. I left the style alone.

summary: Planned a post on connection pooling with the user, choosing three experiments: pool size against throughput, idle timeouts, and what happens when the database restarts.
body:
The user wants the next post to be about connection pooling in front of Postgres, building on the earlier post about indexes. We talked through what a reader would want to learn and settled on three experiments.

The first measures throughput and latency of a small service against pool sizes of 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50, with a database that has 8 cores. The expectation is a plateau after a modest size and worse latency with a very large pool, and the post should show whether the numbers agree. The second experiment looks at idle timeouts: connections that the server or a firewall closes while the pool still thinks they are open, and the errors that follow. The third restarts the database during a run and measures how long the service takes to recover with and without validation of connections on checkout.

I wrote these into the notes file with the questions each should answer, the load for each run and the metric to record. I also listed what is out of scope: external poolers as separate processes are left for a possible follow-up, because comparing them would double the work.

The test harness from the tail latency post can be reused for the load part, so only the service and the database setup are new. I checked that the Postgres version in the homelab is the one the user wants to write about. It is. Next is setting up the test service.

summary: Wrote the connection pooling experiment harness and checked it against a local Postgres, with a baseline of about 4200 queries per second at 20 connections.
body:
After the planning session I built the harness for the three connection pooling experiments. It is a small script in loadtest/pool.py that opens a pool of a chosen size, runs a fixed mix of short queries from 64 worker threads, and writes throughput and latency percentiles to a CSV. The database is a local Postgres in a container with default settings, so the numbers are only comparable with each other.

A first run at 20 connections gave about 4200 queries per second with a p99 of 24 ms. Two repeat runs came within 3 percent of that, which is stable enough to start the sweeps. I added a warm-up of 5 seconds, because the first run without it showed a lower throughput while the pool was still opening connections.

The harness also has two hooks for the later experiments. One sets the server-side idle timeout, and the other restarts the database container in the middle of a run and logs every failed call with its time. I tested the restart hook once with a short run and saw the failures start and stop as expected. The pool size sweep comes next.

summary: Ran the pool size sweep and found throughput flat from 20 connections upward while p99 rose from 24 ms at 20 to 58 ms at 50, so a larger pool only hurt.
body:
I ran the first experiment of the pooling post: pool sizes of 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 with 100 concurrent callers for 60 seconds each, three runs per size, using the median.

Throughput was 390 per second at 2 connections, 950 at 5, 1850 at 10, 3100 at 20 and 3150 at 50. The curve is linear until the database cores are busy and flat after that. The p99 was 210 ms at 2, 96 ms at 5, 49 ms at 10, 24 ms at 20 and 58 ms at 50. So 20 was the best and 50 gave no more work but more waiting inside the database.

I looked at the database during the 50 run. The number of active backends was 50 and CPU was fully used, and context switching rose visibly in the container's stats. That explains the higher p99 without needing a deeper story.

The spread between runs was small, under 4 percent for throughput, but p99 at 50 varied from 51 to 66 ms, so I will present it as about 55 ms and say it was noisy.

One thing to keep honest in the post: the query is almost pure CPU and sleep. A workload that waits on disk would want a larger pool. I added a paragraph in the notes about that, with a rough rule that pool size follows cores plus the share of time spent waiting on I/O.

Results are in results/pool-size.json. Next are the idle timeout errors.

summary: Reproduced the idle connection problem: with the server closing connections after 5 seconds, the pool returned dead ones and 3.1 percent of calls failed until validation was on.
body:
The second experiment needed a server that drops idle connections, so I set idle_session_timeout to 5 seconds in the test database. The pool idle timeout was 30 seconds, so it kept connections that the server had already closed.

The load was bursty: 2 seconds of traffic, 8 seconds of quiet, repeated. After each quiet period the first calls took dead connections and failed with the error terminating connection due to idle-session timeout. Over 10 minutes 3.1 percent of calls failed, all in the first moments after a pause.

Two fixes worked. Setting the pool idle timeout to 4 seconds, below the server's, gave zero failures but made the pool reconnect after every pause, which added about 9 ms to the first calls. Turning on validation at checkout also gave zero failures at a cost of one extra round trip per call, about 0.3 ms.

I put these in the notes as the two options. The post will recommend keeping the pool timeout shorter than anything that closes connections on the other side.

summary: Ran the database restart experiment and found recovery took 14 seconds without validation and 2 seconds with it, with 6400 failed calls against 310.
body:
The third experiment for the pooling post restarts Postgres during a steady load of 1000 requests per second and measures how long the service takes to become healthy again. I ran it with a pool of 20 and compared validation at checkout off and on.

The restart takes about 1.5 seconds in the container. During that time every call fails, which is unavoidable. The difference is what happens after. Without validation, the pool held 20 dead connections, and each failed call discarded only one of them, so errors continued until all had been used up and replaced. The service returned to a zero error rate after 14 seconds, and 6400 calls failed in total over the run.

With validation, the first checkout after the restart found a dead connection, dropped it and tried another, and the whole pool was cleaned in a burst. Recovery took 2 seconds and 310 calls failed, which is close to the restart period itself.

I also tried a third variant, where a failed call causes the whole pool to be flushed. It recovered in 3 seconds with 480 failures and no extra cost on healthy calls, so it is a good option for pools that do not offer validation.

The measurements were taken from the harness output, which records the error rate per second. I made a plot of the error rate over time for the two main variants as a line chart. The no-validation line has a long tail and the validated one drops almost at once. It reads well, so I will use it in the post.

I repeated the run three times and the recovery time varied by about a second in either direction, so I will give rounded values. One caveat: the test used a local container and a restart that finishes quickly. A real failover with a long outage would show the other part of the problem, which is the thundering herd of reconnects, and the post should say it is not covered.

The experiments are now done. Next is a short outline of the post for the user, with the three results in order and the caveats in one section.

summary: Drew the two charts for the connection pooling post, throughput and p99 against pool size and error rate after a restart, as PNG with WebP versions and alt texts.
body:
The user asked for charts before writing, so I made them from the result files.

The first chart has pool size on the horizontal axis, with throughput as a line and p99 as bars. The plateau after 20 connections and the rise of p99 at 50 are both visible. I marked the pool of 20 with a thin vertical line so the eye goes there.

The second chart is the error rate over time after the restart for the two variants, with and without validation. The time axis runs from 0 to 20 seconds and the restart moment is marked. The no-validation line has a tail to 14 seconds, and the other is back to zero at 2.

Both are PNG at 1600 by 900. The files are 52 and 38 KB, and the WebP outputs are 17 and 12 KB. They use the framed background so they look right in dark mode, and I checked this on the archive and on a test page.

The alt texts say what the charts show, including the key numbers. The build check for alt text passes. The scripts are in the charts folder with the data paths, so a redraw takes one command.

summary: Reviewed the user's draft of the connection pooling post and fixed a wrong formula for throughput, a misleading advice line on pool size, and two units.
body:
The user finished the draft of the pooling post and asked me to check it against the experiments.

The formula for the plateau said throughput equals pool size divided by query time, without saying that this holds only until the database cores are busy. That is the whole point of the 20 versus 50 result, so I added the limit and the numbers from the sweep. The advice line said to set the pool as large as the database allows, which contradicts the data, and I replaced it with a starting point of cores plus a small number for I/O waiting, to be tuned by measuring.

Two units were wrong: one said milliseconds where the table had seconds for recovery time, and one said 3100 requests where it meant per second. I fixed both from the result files.

The restart section claimed that validation removes the failures. It reduces them from 6400 to 310, and the remaining ones are the calls that happen while the database is down. I changed the sentence and kept the user's wording otherwise.

I also noticed the section on idle timeouts used the word timeout for three different settings. I suggested naming them: pool idle timeout, server idle session timeout and checkout timeout. The user agreed and will edit that part themselves.

The caveats about the local container and the short outage are in the draft already and read fine. I did not touch the introduction.

summary: Updated dependencies and found that the new Astro minor changed how image cache folders are configured, which made the build time jump from 49 to 78 seconds until the setting was moved.
body:
I ran the routine dependency update. Astro, Tailwind and the highlighter all had minor versions. After the update the build passed, but it took 78 seconds against 49 before, and that looked like the cache problem from earlier in the year.

I checked the output folder. The optimized images were being written again on every build. The cause was a change in where Astro's image service keeps its cache by default: the new version looks in a folder inside node_modules, which Netlify does not keep between builds, and the old setting in the config that pointed to the cache folder was ignored.

The release notes described the new option name. I moved the cache directory setting to it and ran two builds in a row. The first took 80 seconds, and the second took 47, which shows the cache is used.

On Netlify the cache needs the plugin that keeps a folder between builds. The config already listed the old folder, and I checked that the same folder is the one now used. A deploy preview built in 51 seconds after one warm-up build.

Other changes in the update were harmless. The highlighter theme options kept their names this time, and I checked the dark code theme on a post to be sure. Tailwind had one deprecation warning about a class name in the theme, which I fixed.

I checked the feed, the links and the alt text check as usual and they were clean. I added a line to the notes about the cache option name so the next update looks at it first.

summary: Investigated why the RSS feed showed a post twice in one reader and found the reader keyed entries on the link, which changed when a trailing slash was added to the post URLs.
body:
The user got a report from a reader that the pooling post appeared twice in their feed app. I opened the feed and found only one entry for it, so the duplicate came from somewhere else.

The entry id in the feed is the post URL. Looking at the history of the feed config, I found that a change a few weeks ago added a trailing slash to canonical URLs, to match what Netlify serves. The feed items before that change used the address without the slash, and the ones after used it with the slash. The pooling post was published before the change and its feed id was rebuilt afterwards, so a reader that keys on the id saw a new item.

I checked the feed for other posts and found that all items had the new form, so every reader that had stored the old ids could have shown duplicates. The reports are low in number, probably because many readers key on the guid with the permalink flag or on the title and date.

There are two ways to fix it. One is to restore the old ids, which would create duplicates again for readers that already updated. The other is to leave the feed as it is, since it is now stable and consistent. I recommended leaving it and explained the choice to the user, who agreed.

I did add a guard to the build: a small test that compares the feed ids against a stored list and fails if an existing id changes. The list holds all 31 posts. I ran it once against the current feed and it passes. I also wrote a note about the reason in the config file so no one changes the URL form again without thinking about readers.

I told the user what to say to the reader who reported it: mark the duplicate as read, and it will not come back.
